answer:
Most of that weight is the Flutter engine: the browser has no Flutter in it, so every first-time visitor downloads a renderer before your first widget can exist.

### What the build actually ships
- `main.dart.js` — your Dart plus the framework, tree-shaken and minified. Usually the smaller half of the download.
- The renderer. A default build (dart2js) uses **canvaskit**: Skia compiled to WebAssembly, `canvaskit.js` plus `canvaskit.wasm`, a couple of megabytes over the wire. It is fetched from `https://www.gstatic.com/flutter-canvaskit/<engine-hash>/` unless you build with `--no-web-resources-cdn`, and `canvasKitVariant: 'auto'` picks the smaller `chromium` build on Chromium browsers and the `full` one everywhere else.
- **skwasm** is the same Skia compiled to WasmGC, and it only exists in a `--wasm` build, where it can rasterize on a worker thread. It replaces canvaskit for that build; the two do not stack.
- `flutter_bootstrap.js` and `flutter.js` (the loader), `assets/` with `AssetManifest.bin.json`, `FontManifest.json`, `NOTICES` and your own fonts and images.
- There is no lightweight DOM option to fall back to: the HTML renderer was removed in Flutter 3.29.

### What canvas rendering costs on screen
- Text is painted into a canvas, not laid out as DOM. Find-in-page, native text selection and any crawler reading your copy are gone; accessibility comes from a semantics overlay Flutter maintains alongside the canvas.
- A glyph none of your bundled fonts covers triggers a Noto fallback download from `fonts.gstatic.com` at runtime. That is why Cyrillic or emoji sometimes arrive a beat late; `fontFallbackBaseUrl` moves those files to your own host.

The engine is a fixed toll paid on the first visit and free on the next one, so it is priced per visitor rather than per feature. If the page is mostly text that has to load fast for strangers, that toll is the argument against Flutter web, not a number to optimize.
code_example:
flutter build web --release

# build/web
#   index.html                  <base href> and <script src="flutter_bootstrap.js" async>
#   flutter_bootstrap.js        generated per build: build config + the loader
#   flutter.js                  the loader itself, exposes window._flutter
#   main.dart.js                your Dart + the framework, tree-shaken and minified
#   main.dart.js_1.part.js      one per deferred import — only if the split actually worked
#   assets/                     AssetManifest.bin.json, FontManifest.json, fonts/, NOTICES
#   canvaskit/canvaskit.{js,wasm}, canvaskit/chromium/...
#   version.json, manifest.json, favicon.png, icons/

# The local canvaskit/ copy is only a fallback: by default the engine is loaded from
# https://www.gstatic.com/flutter-canvaskit/<engine-hash>/ — one origin you do not control.
flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn    # serve the engine yourself

# dart2wasm + skwasm; still emits the dart2js build beside it as the fallback
flutter build web --release --wasm

# Measure what actually crosses the wire, not what is on disk
ls -lh build/web/main.dart.js
gzip -9 -c build/web/canvaskit/canvaskit.wasm | wc -c
gzip -9 -c build/web/main.dart.js | wc -c

answer:
Because `--wasm` is opt-in and still emits JavaScript beside the wasm: Flutter builds both outputs into one deploy and the loader picks at runtime, so JS is what a large share of your users actually run.

### What the wasm build buys
- `dart2wasm` compiles Dart to WasmGC and pairs with the skwasm renderer, which rasterizes on a worker thread. Google's published numbers are roughly 2x faster frame times and ~2.5x faster widget building, with total bundle size within about 5% of the JS build.
- Multi-threaded rendering only switches on when the server sends `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless` (or `require-corp`) and `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`. Miss them and you silently get single-threaded skwasm, not an error.
- If WasmGC is not detected at runtime the dart2js output runs instead, from the same `build/web`. One deploy serves both; `kIsWasm` (`bool.fromEnvironment('dart.tool.dart2wasm')`) tells your code which one it got.

### Why it is not the default yet
- It needs WasmGC. Chromium has had it since 119, but Flutter's docs still list Firefox and Safari as blocked by engine bugs against the wasm renderer, and no browser on iOS can run it at all — they are all required to use WebKit.
- The compiler is stricter about interop. `dart:html`, `dart:js` and `package:js` do not exist for dart2wasm; one transitive dependency still on them fails the build. `package:web` and `dart:js_interop` are the replacements.
- Deferred loading is experimental on wasm (`--enable-wasm-deferred-loading`, targeted to be generally available in 3.50), so code that splits cleanly under dart2js can ship as a single module under dart2wasm.

Treat wasm as a progressive enhancement you can turn on today: audit the dependency tree for legacy interop first, add the two headers, and keep the JS build as the floor rather than a fallback you hope nobody hits.

Four stages, and nothing you write in Dart can paint before all of them finish: the HTML loads, `flutter_bootstrap.js` chooses a build, the entrypoint and the engine download, and only then does `runApp` produce a frame.

### The sequence
1. `index.html` runs `flutter_bootstrap.js` — generated per build, carrying the build config: which outputs exist, which renderer and compile target each one is for. The `{{flutter_bootstrap_js}}` token inlines it so it costs no extra request.
2. `_flutter.loader.load()` picks a build this browser can run, then fetches `main.dart.js` (or `main.dart.wasm`) and the renderer — `canvaskit.wasm` from gstatic by default, or skwasm.
3. `engineInitializer.initializeEngine()` creates the view and the canvas and wires up the platform bindings.
4. `appRunner.runApp()` starts Dart `main()`. Your first frame is the first pixel the user sees.

### Where the seconds go
- Every byte is on the critical path, so the wins are overlap and transport, not micro-optimisation: preload the entrypoint and the engine, serve them from your own origin over HTTP/2 with brotli, and give them long cache lifetimes.
- Put a real skeleton — markup and CSS in `index.html`, not a spinner — and remove it once the app is up. From Dart the honest signal is a post-frame callback after the first frame; from JS it is the promise `runApp()` returns.
- Do not await work in `main()` before `runApp`. A config fetch, Firebase init or a plugin warm-up there extends the white screen by exactly its own duration. Start them after the first frame and show a loading state built from widgets.
- Measure against a release build in the browser's performance panel. Flutter DevTools sees nothing before the engine boots, which is where most of the two seconds are.

First paint on web is a network problem, then a boot problem, and only a distant third a Flutter problem.

dart2js moves a library into its own part file only when every path to it is deferred; one ordinary import anywhere in the program pulls the whole thing back into the main output unit.

### How the split is actually computed
- `import 'admin/admin.dart' deferred as admin;` plus `await admin.loadLibrary();` makes dart2js emit `main.dart.js_1.part.js`, fetched on that call. `loadLibrary()` is idempotent and returns a Future you can await again; on a network failure it rejects, so deferred code needs a real error state, not just a spinner.
- Loading units are computed over the whole program, not per import. Anything reachable from both the eager entrypoint and the deferred library stays in the main unit — which is usually correct, since your models, theme and shared widgets really are used by both, and it is why a "400 KB feature" often frees only a fraction of that.
- The usual leaks: a route table that names `AdminPage` directly, a barrel file re-exported from somewhere eager, a service locator registering the type at startup, or a `const` or enum from the deferred library referenced at top level.

### Verify it, and mind the wasm caveat
- Check `build/web` for `main.dart.js_*.part.js` files and their sizes. No part files means nothing split, whatever the source looks like. Compare real byte sizes before and after, not your intent.
- On a `--wasm` build deferred loading is experimental behind `--enable-wasm-deferred-loading` (targeted for general availability in 3.50), so the same code can split under dart2js and ship as one module under dart2wasm.
- `deferred-components` in `pubspec.yaml` is the Android app-bundle feature and does nothing for web. On web the mechanism is only the Dart-level deferred import.

Split at seams where the dependency graph genuinely forks — a screen that drags in a chart library, a PDF viewer, a rich text editor — not at whichever screen looks big in your editor.

Three separate things are broken and each has its own fix: the URL strategy in Dart, `<base href>` in the built HTML, and a server that must return `index.html` for paths with no file behind them.

### The three fixes
- **URL strategy.** The default is the hash strategy, `/console/#/settings`, and the server never sees anything after the `#`. Calling `usePathUrlStrategy()` from `package:flutter_web_plugins/url_strategy.dart` before `runApp()` switches to real paths — and hands you the 404 problem, because now the server does see them.
- **base href.** Every relative URL — `main.dart.js`, `assets/...`, the manifest — resolves against `<base href>`, not against the current path. At `/console/settings/42` with `<base href="/">` the browser asks for `/console/settings/assets/...` and gets nothing. Build with `flutter build web --base-href /console/`; the value must start and end with a slash.
- **Server rewrite.** `GET /console/settings/42` has no file. Firebase Hosting calls it a single-page app; nginx is `try_files $uri $uri/ /console/index.html`. GitHub Pages has no rewrite at all, so the usual trick is to deploy a copy of `index.html` as `404.html` and let the router read the path it was asked for.

### The redirect that bites afterwards
- Static hosts often 301 a path to or from a trailing slash. That redirect happens before Flutter runs, so a link people share can arrive at a different path than the one you routed for, and `go_router`'s `redirect` sees the rewritten URL. Pick one canonical form and make the router treat both as the same route.
- `flutter run -d chrome` falls back to `index.html` for every path, which is exactly why this class of bug only ever shows up after deploying.

When you cannot control the server — a kiosk build, an embed, something opened from disk — keep the hash strategy. It is ugly in the address bar and it always works.

Nothing from inside the Flutter app: your content is painted into a canvas and your `<head>` is one static file, so a crawler and a link scraper both receive the same empty shell no matter which route was requested.

### What a bot actually receives
- Flutter draws glyphs, not DOM text. Googlebot does execute JavaScript and can render the shell, but there is no heading structure, no copy and no per-route `<title>` for it to index. Flutter's own web FAQ says plainly that the framework is not aimed at SEO and points at Jaspr for Dart-authored static sites.
- Link scrapers — Slack, WhatsApp, iMessage, X — do not run JavaScript at all. They read the Open Graph tags in the HTML they got back, which is the single `index.html` your build produced, so every URL previews identically.
- The semantics tree is an accessibility overlay Flutter builds on demand. It is not markup, and it is not what a crawler treats as your page content.

### The options, in the order I would try them
- Move the pages that must be found out of Flutter. Marketing pages, docs and blog posts are documents; serve them as HTML from the same domain and keep Flutter for the app behind the login.
- Put a hosting rewrite or an edge function in front of the app that injects a per-route `<title>` and `og:` tags into `index.html` before it is served. That fixes previews for every scraper and gives crawlers something to file, without touching a line of Dart.
- Prerender only if you must — a headless browser producing HTML per route, served to bots — knowing you now maintain a second rendering of every page and a cache-invalidation story to go with it.
- Use the path URL strategy and publish a sitemap either way; none of the above works while every route lives behind a `#`.

Flutter web is for the app behind the login. A page that has to be found by a search engine is a document problem, and documents are what HTML is for.
code_example:
# What a scraper sees: the same shell for every route
curl -s https://app.example.com/pricing | grep -iE '<title>|og:title|og:description'
# <title>app</title>          <- identical for /pricing, /blog/x, /login

# Fix at the edge, not in Dart: generate one shell per route at deploy time
build_shell() {                       # $1 = route, $2 = title, $3 = description
  mkdir -p "build/web$1"
  sed -e "s|<title>app</title>|<title>$2</title>|" \
      -e "s|</head>|<meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"$2\">\n<meta property=\"og:description\" content=\"$3\">\n<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://app.example.com$1\">\n</head>|" \
      build/web/index.html > "build/web$1/index.html"
}

flutter build web --release
build_shell /pricing "Pricing — Acme" "Plans that start free."
build_shell /changelog "Changelog — Acme" "What shipped this month."

# Every generated shell still boots the same Flutter app; only the head differs.
# The router reads the path, so the user lands on the right screen.

# A sitemap the crawler can follow, since it cannot discover in-canvas links
{
  echo '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>'
  echo '<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">'
  for p in / /pricing /changelog; do
    echo "  <url><loc>https://app.example.com$p</loc></url>"
  done
  echo '</urlset>'
} > build/web/sitemap.xml

# Verify with the tool the platform actually uses, not with your browser
curl -s -A 'Twitterbot/1.0' https://app.example.com/pricing | grep og:title

From caching you now own yourself: recent Flutter versions stopped generating `flutter_service_worker.js` and the loader no longer registers any worker, so what is left is the plain HTTP cache — plus, on long-time users' machines, the old worker that is still installed.

### The HTTP cache, which is now the whole story
- `flutter build web` emits unhashed filenames. `index.html`, `flutter_bootstrap.js` and `main.dart.js` keep their names across every deploy, so a long `max-age` on them serves stale code until it expires, and nothing invalidates it for you.
- Serve `index.html` and `flutter_bootstrap.js` with `Cache-Control: no-cache` — that means revalidate every time, not "do not store", and a 304 costs nothing when the file has not changed. Engine files under the versioned `flutter-canvaskit/<hash>/` URL are genuinely immutable; your own `main.dart.js` needs revalidation unless your host fingerprints it.
- Delete leftovers from an old `index.html` template: `var serviceWorkerVersion = null;` and `serviceWorkerSettings` in the loader config no longer do anything.

### The worker that is still installed
- A service worker registered by an older build keeps serving its cached app shell indefinitely; those users never even request your new `index.html`. Removing the file from the deploy does not unregister it — the browser keeps running the last copy it saw.
- Ship a tombstone at the same URL that unregisters itself, deletes its caches and reloads its clients, and keep it deployed for as long as your tail of returning users lasts.
- If you want offline support or an "update available" prompt, that is yours to write now — Workbox or a hand-rolled worker — including the update UX: detect `registration.waiting`, ask the user, `skipWaiting()`, reload on `controllerchange`.

There is no store review on web, so nothing stands between your fix and your users except a cache header you chose. Decide it deliberately and verify it with a request, not with a hard refresh.

Because `kIsWeb` is a runtime constant inside a file that has already imported `dart:io`, and `dart:io` does not exist on web — the build fails at the import, long before your branch could be eliminated.

### Split the file, not the branch
- Conditional imports choose a *file* per compile target: `import 'store_stub.dart' if (dart.library.io) 'store_io.dart' if (dart.library.js_interop) 'store_web.dart';` Only the selected file is compiled, so `dart:io` never reaches the web build.
- The default — the stub — is what the analyzer type-checks against, so all three files must expose the same API. Keep it to one factory function or one class with identical signatures and the whole thing stays strictly typed; there is never a reason for `dynamic` or a cast here.
- Condition on `dart.library.js_interop`, not `dart.library.html`. `dart:html` is gone for dart2wasm, so a condition on it silently selects the stub in exactly the build you were trying to support.
- `dart.library.io` is true for Android, iOS, Windows, macOS and Linux, which is usually what you want: one native implementation, one web implementation.

### What kIsWeb and defaultTargetPlatform are actually for
- `kIsWeb` is a `const bool`, so `if (kIsWeb)` really is dead-code eliminated. Use it for behaviour in code that already compiles everywhere: skip a biometric prompt, drop a swipe-to-dismiss gesture, choose a different upload flow.
- `defaultTargetPlatform` on web reports the host OS of the *browser*: a Chrome tab on a Mac reports `TargetPlatform.macOS`, Safari on an iPhone reports `iOS`. That is right for scroll physics and Cupertino styling and wrong for anything meaning "a native app" — check `kIsWeb` first.
- `Platform.isIOS` is `dart:io`, and reaching for it is exactly how the forbidden import creeps back in.

One rule: a platform *API* goes behind a conditional import, a platform *behaviour* goes behind `kIsWeb` or `defaultTargetPlatform`.

`dart:html`, `dart:js` and `dart:js_util` are deprecated and unsupported under dart2wasm: the DOM now comes from `package:web`, and everything else goes through `dart:js_interop`.

### The two halves
- **package:web** is a generated, typed binding to the browser IDL — `web.document.querySelector('#root')`, `web.window.localStorage`. Names follow the spec rather than the old Dart-ified ones (`HTMLAnchorElement`, `classList`), so most of the migration is renaming.
- **dart:js_interop** describes JS values: `JSObject`, `JSString`, `JSPromise`, `JSFunction`. You declare what JS provides as `external` members on a top-level `@JS()` declaration or on an `extension type` over `JSObject` — an extension type is a compile-time view, so no wrapper object is allocated at runtime.

### Crossing the boundary
- Conversions are explicit and one call each: `'x'.toJS`, `jsString.toDart`, `await promise.toDart`, `callback.toJS`, plus `jsify()`/`dartify()` for loose data with no schema worth typing.
- `globalContext` is `globalThis`, and `importModule('./sdk.js').toDart` pulls in an ES module at runtime instead of a `<script>` tag.

### What catches people
- Interop members must be `external`, and you cannot bolt them onto an ordinary class — a wrapper either holds a `JSObject` field or is an extension type.
- `JSObject` carries no Dart type identity, so `is` and `as` between interop types prove nothing; ask `value.isA<JSArray>()` instead.
- The declared types are erased. An `external` method annotated as returning `String` will hand you `undefined` if the SDK changes, so validate at the boundary exactly as you validate JSON.

Flutter web mounts into whatever element you hand the loader through `hostElement`, and the two sides exchange data only through explicit JS interop — there is no shared state, no shared router and no shared event bus.

### Mounting into an element
- The build emits `flutter_bootstrap.js`; drop your own copy in `web/` using the `{{flutter_js}}` and `{{flutter_build_config}}` tokens and call `_flutter.loader.load({config: {hostElement: el}})`.
- Without `hostElement` Flutter takes over `<body>`, and the host page stops receiving pointer events entirely.
- The host element needs a real size. Flutter fills it, so a `div` with no height renders nothing and looks like a failed load.

### Data in both directions
- **JS to Dart**: at startup install a Dart closure on `globalContext` and push what arrives into a `ValueNotifier` or a stream. For values known at mount time, pass `initialData` to `addView` and read it with `ui_web.views.getInitialData(viewId)`.
- **Dart to JS**: either call an `external` function the host defined, or dispatch a `CustomEvent` on the host element so the page listens with `addEventListener` like it does for any other component.
- Convert at the edge. Domain objects stay Dart-side; what crosses is `JSString`, `JSNumber` and jsified maps.

### Traps
- One engine per app instance: two separate mounts download and boot CanvasKit twice. For two regions on one page use multi-view — `multiViewEnabled: true`, `runWidget`, and a `View` per entry in `PlatformDispatcher.views`.
- The embedded app still owns the address bar unless you call `setUrlStrategy(null)`, and it will fight the host's router.
- First paint still costs the whole engine download. For a widget-sized feature that is usually the argument against embedding at all.

Almost none of the window is Dart: the first window is created by the native runner checked into your own repo, menus and exit handling are framework APIs, and everything you want to change at runtime is a package.

### The runner owns the first frame
- Initial size and position live in `windows/runner/main.cpp` (`Win32Window::Size size(1280, 800)`), `macos/Runner/MainFlutterWindow.swift` (`self.setFrame`) and `linux/runner/my_application.cc` (`gtk_window_set_default_size`). They are your source files — edit them.
- Resizing from Dart on the first frame instead gives users a visible jump. The generated Windows runner already waits for Flutter's first frame before calling `Show()`, which is what keeps the white flash away.

### What the framework does give you
- `PlatformMenuBar` with `PlatformMenu`/`PlatformMenuItem` builds a real macOS menu bar; macOS is the only platform with a delegate, elsewhere it just renders its child. For an in-app menu on Windows and Linux use Material's `MenuBar`, `SubmenuButton` and `MenuItemButton`.
- `AppLifecycleListener(onExitRequested:)` intercepts Cmd+Q, the taskbar close and OS shutdown; return `AppExitResponse.cancel` to show a save prompt, then quit through `ServicesBinding.instance.exitApplication`.

### What is still a package
- `window_manager` for runtime size, minimum size, centring, always-on-top, full screen and close interception; `tray_manager` for a tray icon and its menu; `screen_retriever` for display and DPI.
- Several real OS windows is the newest gap: the framework's multi-window API (`runWidget` with `RegularWindow`) is experimental behind a flag, and shipping apps still use `desktop_multi_window`, which starts a second engine — separate isolate, separate state, a method channel between them.

Rule of thumb: before `runApp` it is the runner, menus and exit are framework, the rest of the window is a package.

There is no filesystem on the web: `dart:io` and `path_provider` do not exist there, so a save is a download and every read starts from a file the user personally handed you in a gesture.

### Reading
- `file_selector` and `file_picker` return an `XFile` on every platform, and `readAsBytes()` is the only portable call on it. `XFile.path` is a real path on desktop and a `blob:` URL on the web, so any code that opens the path breaks there.
- Files dropped from the OS need a package: `super_drag_and_drop` covers web and desktop, `desktop_drop` desktop only. Flutter's own `DragTarget` moves widgets inside the app and never sees an OS drag.

### Writing
- Desktop: `getSaveLocation()` for the path, then `dart:io` behind a conditional import.
- Web: build a `Blob`, make an object URL and click a synthetic anchor, or use `showSaveFilePicker` — Chromium only, secure context only. Both must run inside the same task as the user's click; `await` a network call first and the popup blocker eats it.

### The sandbox
- `Clipboard.setData` works everywhere, reading does not: `Clipboard.getData` on the web maps to `navigator.clipboard.readText`, which needs a permission and a gesture and is restricted in Safari and Firefox. Images and HTML are not in `Clipboard` at all — that is `super_clipboard`.
- The macOS runner ships with App Sandbox enabled, so you may only touch what the picker returned. Add `com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-write` to both entitlement files, and store a security-scoped bookmark if you want to reopen that file tomorrow.

Rule of thumb: on the web the gesture is the permission — you get exactly the file the user pointed at, for exactly as long as the page lives.

A key event goes from `HardwareKeyboard` to the primary focus and then *up* the focus chain: the first `Shortcuts` on that path that matches turns it into an `Intent`, and the first enabled `Action` for that Intent type above it runs — so both bugs are about where your `Shortcuts` sits relative to focus.

### The route, in order
1. `HardwareKeyboard` dispatches a `KeyEvent`. The old `RawKeyEvent` and `RawKeyboardListener` are deprecated — use `KeyboardListener` and `HardwareKeyboard.instance`.
2. `FocusManager` walks from the primary focus up through its ancestors, offering the event to each `Focus`.
3. A `Shortcuts` on that path matches a `ShortcutActivator` and dispatches the `Intent`.
4. `Actions.invoke` walks up again for an `Action` of that Intent type whose `isEnabled` returns true.

### Why the dialog kills it
A route pushed by `Navigator` is a sibling of your page inside the `Overlay`, not a descendant of it. Focus moves into the dialog, your page's `Shortcuts` is no longer on the chain, and the binding is simply gone. App-wide shortcuts belong above the `Navigator` — `MaterialApp.shortcuts` and `MaterialApp.actions`, or a `Shortcuts` wrapping the whole app — and only page-specific ones live on the page.

### Why it fires mid-word
Character keys still travel up the focus chain past a focused `TextField`, so a bare-letter activator triggers while the user types. Wrap the field in a `Shortcuts` mapping those activators to `DoNothingAndStopPropagationIntent`, or make the `Action.isEnabled` false while an `EditableText` holds focus.

There is no "platform modifier": write `SingleActivator(key, control: !isMac, meta: isMac)`, and prefer `SingleActivator` over `LogicalKeySet` so repeats and modifier strictness are yours to set.

Audit platform support as data before the first build, because a missing implementation surfaces in three different places — a failed build, a `MissingPluginException` on the first call, or a silent no-op — and only the first one is loud.

### How a plugin declares its platforms
- Plugins are federated: `foo` is app-facing, `foo_platform_interface` is the contract, `foo_web` and `foo_windows` are implementations. The platform chips on pub.dev come from the `flutter: plugin: platforms:` map in the pubspec.
- An implementation only registers automatically if the app-facing package **endorses** it. A community `foo_web` that is not endorsed must be added to your own `pubspec.yaml`, or nothing is ever registered and you get `MissingPluginException` at runtime.

### Finding the gaps before QA
- Build every target you ship on every pull request. Compile-time gaps are the cheap kind: a dependency that imports `dart:io` fails `flutter build web` immediately.
- Runtime gaps need execution. Extend the integration run to Chrome and one desktop target and actually open the screens that call plugins; a build that succeeds proves nothing about a channel that has no receiver.
- `flutter pub deps --style=compact` gives the list to check; do it once and record the verdict per plugin in the repo, because the next upgrade can change it.

### Degrading in the widget tree
- Put each shaky capability behind a small facade with `bool get isSupported` and one call. The tree asks the facade and renders the alternative — no Scan QR button, a manual entry field instead.
- Do not wrap every call site in `try/catch (MissingPluginException)`. An exception is not a feature flag; it fires after the user has already tapped.

Rule of thumb: a feature that cannot exist on a platform should be absent from the tree there, not a button that throws.

Each OS wants its own signature and its own package: a signed MSIX or installer on Windows, a Developer ID build with the hardened runtime that is notarised and stapled on macOS, and a distro package or Flatpak on Linux — and the updater is entirely yours to build.

### Windows
- `flutter build windows --release` leaves an executable next to `flutter_windows.dll`, the plugin DLLs and `data/`. Ship the whole folder; the `.exe` alone starts and immediately dies.
- `dart run msix:create` packages that folder as MSIX from a `msix_config:` block in `pubspec.yaml`. A certificate from a public CA is what stops the SmartScreen warning — a self-signed one only works if you also push the root through MDM. Inno Setup is the usual alternative when MSIX containerisation gets in the way.

### macOS
- Sign with a Developer ID Application identity and the hardened runtime, submit with `xcrun notarytool submit --wait`, then `xcrun stapler staple`. An unstapled app shows "damaged and can't be opened" to anyone offline.
- Entitlements are per configuration. The release build has its own `Release.entitlements`, and `com.apple.security.network.client` is not in it by default — networking works all through development and dies in the shipped build.

### Linux and updating
- `flutter build linux --release` produces a bundle tied to the GTK and glibc of the machine that built it. Build in a container matching the oldest distro you support, then wrap it as `.deb`, Flatpak or AppImage.
- Flutter has no updater. `auto_updater` wraps Sparkle and WinSparkle against an appcast XML you host; MSIX has App Installer; on Linux the package manager is the updater. Whichever you pick, the client must verify a signature, not just compare a version string.
code_example:
# --- Windows ---------------------------------------------------------------
flutter build windows --release

signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 \

flutter build macos --release
codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
  --sign "Developer ID Application: Acme GmbH (TEAMID)" \
  build/macos/Build/Products/Release/Ledger.app

ditto -c -k --keepParent Ledger.app Ledger.zip

xcrun stapler staple Ledger.app   # skip this and offline users see "damaged"

That message is the browser refusing to let Dart see the response, and it is almost always CORS — the exception carries no status because your code never received one.

### What the browser is doing
- It attaches `Origin` to the request, and for anything beyond a simple request — a JSON content type, an `Authorization` header — it sends an `OPTIONS` preflight first.
- The server must answer with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Methods` and `-Headers`. With cookies you also need `Allow-Credentials: true` and a concrete origin, because the wildcard is illegal alongside credentials.
- No Dart change fixes it. `package:http` on the web is the browser's own fetch stack, and the real reason is printed in the Console tab, never in the Dart stack. Mixed content — an `http://` call from an `https://` page — produces the same useless exception.

### Getting a real stack out of a release build
- `flutter build web --release --source-maps` emits `main.dart.js.map`, and devtools then shows Dart file and line instead of minified frames. Upload the map to your error tracker rather than serving it publicly if the source is sensitive.
- Uncaught errors only reach the tracker if you install both `FlutterError.onError` and `PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError`.

### Reproducing it locally
- Serve the built output with a static server at the same `--base-href` the host uses, because a path bug looks exactly like a broken app.
- Unregister the service worker first. A stale one happily serves yesterday's `main.dart.js`, and you will debug code that is not deployed.
- `--web-browser-flag "--disable-web-security"` confirms a CORS diagnosis in ten seconds and is never a fix; a dev proxy on the same origin is.
